extracted.intended_audience: general readers of classic literature / readers of Don Quixote
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter excerpt from Cervantes' Don Quixote (translation) containing narrative dialogue and authorial asides about history-writing, poetry, reputation, and plans for adventures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historian must write truthfully
rubrics_metrics.description: “the historian has to write them down, not as they ought to have been, but as they were, without adding anything to the truth or taking anything from it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History is described as 'in a measure a sacred thing, for it should be true, and where the truth is, there God is.' The text condemns historians who resort to falsehood: "historians who have recourse to falsehood ought to be burned, like those who coin false money."

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet may embellish (poetic license)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the poet may describe or sing things, not as they were, but as they ought to have been.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes genres: poets can alter or idealize events for effect, whereas historians must stick to factual truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrelevant digressions/inserted novels
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the faults they find with this history is that its author inserted in it a novel called 'The Ill-advised Curiosity' ... not that it is bad or ill-told, but that it is out of place and has nothing to do with the history of his worship Señor Don Quixote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid including unrelated episodes that distract from or do not serve the main historical/narrative thread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit humiliating details that don't affect truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “there is no need of recording events which do not change or affect the truth of a history, if they tend to bring the hero of it into contempt.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer relevance over exhaustive recording when details only serve to degrade the subject without altering the factual account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide completeness; avoid unexplained omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics complain the author 'forgot to say who the thief was who stole Sancho’s Dapple' and 'forgot to state what Sancho did with those hundred crowns'—omissions seen as serious faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Histories/narratives should account for earlier-mentioned matters and avoid unexplained discontinuities that leave readers puzzled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed works are more closely scrutinized; publish carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: “as printed works are examined leisurely, their faults are easily seen; and the greater the fame of the writer, the more closely are they scrutinised.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication increases exposure to criticism and can damage reputation if the work is flawed; therefore, extra care is needed before printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing requires great judgment and ripe understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: “to write histories, or books of any kind, there is need of great judgment and a ripe understanding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should bring maturity, discernment, and intellectual skill to composition; shallow or hasty authorship is faulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective humour and comic character require skill
rubrics_metrics.description: “To give expression to humour, and write in a strain of graceful pleasantry, is the gift of great geniuses. The cleverest character in comedy is the clown, for he who would make people take him for a fool, must not be one.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful comic writing and performance depend on intelligence, artifice, and restraint rather than mere buffoonery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain moral propriety; avoid immodesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The bachelor praises the history as 'the most delightful and least injurious entertainment... there is not to be found in the whole of it even the semblance of an immodest word, or a thought that is other than Catholic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this cultural/authorial context, acceptable entertainment should avoid immodest content and maintain moral decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrained poetic composition (acrostic requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don Quixote requests verses in which 'a letter of her name was placed at the beginning of each line, so that, at the end of the verses, "Dulcinea del Toboso" might be read by putting together the first letters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical compositional constraint: number of letters (17) must be reconciled with stanza structure (e.g., four ballad stanzas of four lines leaves one letter over), so the poet must choose stanza form or drop letters to satisfy the acrostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hasty, profit-driven composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The bachelor reports the author is 'moved more by the profit that may accrue to him from doing so than by any thought of praise' and Sancho warns 'works done in a hurry are never finished as perfectly as they ought to be.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rushed composition for money tends to reduce quality; authors should prioritize care over speed/profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and withstand envious criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Men famous for their genius... are always, or most commonly, envied by those who take a particular delight and pleasure in criticising the writings of others, without having produced any of their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Famous authors should anticipate detractors and not be unduly troubled by criticism from those who have produced nothing comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as qualification for office (governors must know grammar)
rubrics_metrics.description: On governing islands: 'those that govern islands must at least know grammar.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented in dialogue partly jesting, but asserted as a qualification — literacy/education (grammar) is expected of officials.
